cells.label: manual
cells.bodyHtml: No service worker support documented; the public assets guide shows only a <link rel="manifest"> tag. Hand-write the worker in public/ and register it from a client component. (public-assets)
cells.exampleHtml:
Put a hand-written worker in public/ and register it from a client component rendered on every page.

// public/sw.js
const CACHE = "app-v1"; // change the name on each deploy

self.addEventListener("fetch", (event) => {
  const { request } = event;
  if (request.method !== "GET" || new URL(request.url).origin !== location.origin) return;
  // Network first, so pages stay current. The cached copy answers when offline.
  event.respondWith(
    fetch(request)
      .then((response) => {
        const copy = response.clone();
        caches.open(CACHE).then((cache) => cache.put(request, copy));
        return response;
      })
      .catch(() => caches.match(request)),
  );
});
// src/app/components/RegisterServiceWorker.tsx
"use client";
import { useEffect } from "react";

export function RegisterServiceWorker() {
  useEffect(() => {
    if ("serviceWorker" in navigator) navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js");
  }, []);
  return null;
}

Source: Using Service Workers (MDN) · RedwoodSDK: Public Assets

cells.label: first-party
cells.bodyHtml: Styles written with the css(...) mixin from remix/component are collected during server rendering, deduplicated and emitted as <style data-rmx-style> tags in the document head. Global stylesheets added with <link rel="stylesheet"> and assets.getHref() stay linked files. (rendering-ui, component)
cells.exampleHtml:
Styles written with css(...) and applied through the mix prop are collected during server rendering. Remix dedupes them and writes them into <style data-rmx-style> tags in the document head.

// app/ui/book-card.tsx
import { css } from "remix/component";
import type { Handle } from "remix/component";

export function BookCard(handle: Handle<{ title: string; author: string }>) {
  return () => (
    <article
      mix={css({
        border: "1px solid #d6d6d6",
        borderRadius: "12px",
        padding: "1rem",
        "&:hover": { borderColor: "#6d28d9" },
        "@media (max-width: 40rem)": { borderRadius: 0 },
      })}
    >
      <h2>{handle.props.title}</h2>
      <p>{handle.props.author}</p>
    </article>
  );
}

Source: Remix: Rendering UI, styling with css

cells.label: third-party
cells.bodyHtml: No first-party font module documented. The asset server rewrites url() references in CSS, and a font preload is a hand-written <link rel="preload" as="font"> using assets.getHref(); the third-party route is Fontsource. (files-and-assets)
cells.exampleHtml:
Install Fontsource, allow the package in the asset server, and link its stylesheet. The asset server rewrites the url() references in the CSS. The preload is a hand-written <link> with a URL from getHref().

// app/assets.ts  (npm i @fontsource-variable/inter)
export const assets = createAssetServer({
  // …
  allowPackages: ["remix", "@fontsource-variable/inter"],
  files: { extensions: [".svg", ".png", ".jpg", ".woff2"] },
});

export const fontCssHref = await assets.getHref(
  "node_modules/@fontsource-variable/inter/index.css",
);
export const fontHref = await assets.getHref(
  "node_modules/@fontsource-variable/inter/files/inter-latin-wght-normal.woff2",
);

// app/actions/document.tsx, inside <head>
<link rel="preload" href={fontHref} as="font" type="font/woff2" crossOrigin="anonymous" />
<link rel="stylesheet" href={fontCssHref} />

Source: Remix: Files and assets, reference styles, images, and fonts

cells.label: third-party
cells.bodyHtml: The asset server has a first-party transform pipeline: files.transforms defined with defineFileTransform, requested as assets.getHref(path, { transform: [["resize", "400"], "webp"] }), with createFsFileCache() for results. The resize and format code is written by the app with the third-party Sharp library, and there is no image component or srcset helper. (files-and-assets, assets)
cells.exampleHtml:
The asset server runs named file transforms that the app writes with Sharp. A URL picks the chain, and createFsFileCache() keeps the results on disk.

// app/assets.ts  (npm i sharp)
import { createAssetServer, createFsFileCache, defineFileTransform } from "remix/assets";
import sharp from "sharp";

export const assets = createAssetServer({
  // …
  files: {
    extensions: [".png", ".jpg"],
    transforms: {
      resize: defineFileTransform({
        extensions: [".png", ".jpg"],
        param: true,
        // check that param is a width in range before using it
        transform: (bytes, { param }) => sharp(bytes).resize({ width: Number(param) }).toBuffer(),
      }),
      webp: defineFileTransform({
        extensions: [".png", ".jpg"],
        transform: async (bytes) => ({ content: await sharp(bytes).webp().toBuffer(), extension: ".webp" }),
      }),
    },
    cache: createFsFileCache(),
  },
});

// in an action
let coverHref = await assets.getHref("app/ui/public/cover.jpg", { transform: [["resize", "400"], "webp"] });

Source: Remix: Files and assets, transform images and other files

artDirection.label: manual
artDirection.bodyHtml: No first-party <picture> helper documented; hand-write <picture> with transform URLs from assets.getHref(). (files-and-assets)
artDirection.exampleHtml:
There is no image component, so write <picture> yourself. Resolve each crop and format with assets.getHref() transforms in the action and pass the URLs in as props.

// app/ui/hero-image.tsx
import type { Handle } from "remix/component";
import { assets } from "../assets.ts";

export async function getHeroSources() {
  let get = (file: string, transform: (string | [string, string])[]) => assets.getHref(`app/ui/public/${file}`, { transform });
  return {
    square: await get("hero-square.jpg", [["resize", "640"], "webp"]),
    wide: await get("hero-wide.jpg", [["resize", "1280"], "webp"]),
    fallback: await get("hero-wide.jpg", [["resize", "1280"]]),
  };
}

export function HeroImage(handle: Handle<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof getHeroSources>>>) {
  return () => (
    <picture>
      {/* art direction: a square crop on narrow screens */}
      <source media="(max-width: 640px)" type="image/webp" srcset={handle.props.square} />
      <source type="image/webp" srcset={handle.props.wide} />
      <img src={handle.props.fallback} alt="Shelves of books" width={1280} height={720}
           fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" />
    </picture>
  );
}

Source: Remix: Files and assets, transform images and other files

cells.label: manual
cells.bodyHtml: No prerender, ISR or data cache documented; actions return standard Response objects and set Cache-Control by hand. Fingerprinted assets are served with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. (request-handling, assets)
cells.exampleHtml:
There is no data or HTML cache, so each action sets Cache-Control on its own response. context.render() takes a ResponseInit for that.

// app/actions/books/controller.tsx
import { createController } from "remix/router";
import { routes } from "../../routes.ts";
import { getBook } from "./data.ts";
import { BookPage } from "./show-page.tsx";

export default createController(routes.books, {
  actions: {
    async show(context) {
      let book = await getBook(context.params.bookId);
      if (!book) return new Response("Book not found", { status: 404 });

      return context.render(<BookPage book={book} />, {
        headers: { "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=600" },
      });
    },
  },
});

Source: Remix: Rendering UI, rendering pages through request context

cells.label: first-party
cells.bodyHtml: <a href="/products/shirt" data-rmx-prefetch="intent"> or "viewport" loads the destination before navigation; prefetch() from remix/component does it from code. (component, interactivity)
cells.exampleHtml:
Add data-rmx-prefetch to a link to load the destination on hover or focus (intent) or when it scrolls into view (viewport). prefetch() does the same from code.

// app/ui/book-link.tsx
import { prefetch } from "remix/component";
import type { Handle } from "remix/component";
import { routes } from "../routes.ts";

export function BookLink(handle: Handle<{ bookId: string; title: string }>) {
  return () => (
    <a href={routes.books.show.href({ bookId: handle.props.bookId })} data-rmx-prefetch="intent">
      {handle.props.title}
    </a>
  );
}

// elsewhere, from custom logic
prefetch(routes.books.show.href({ bookId: "dune" }));

Source: Remix: Interactivity, prefetch links before navigation

cells.label: first-party
cells.bodyHtml: Give a <Frame src="..."> a fallback; the fallback is part of the initial HTML, and when the frame's route finishes Remix streams its HTML and replaces the fallback. The render() middleware from remix/middleware/render streams the component tree. A frame without a fallback blocks the first chunk. (streaming-ui-with-frames)
cells.exampleHtml:
The render() middleware streams the component tree. A <Frame> with a fallback sends the fallback in the first chunk, then streams the frame route's HTML when it is ready.

// app/router.ts
import { render } from "remix/middleware/render";
import { createRouter } from "remix/router";
import { assets } from "./assets.ts";

export const router = createRouter({
  middleware: [render({ assets })],
});

// app/actions/books/show-page.tsx
<main>
  <h1>{book.title}</h1>
  <Frame
    src={routes.books.reviews.href({ bookId: book.id })}
    fallback={<p>Loading reviews…</p>}
  />
</main>

Source: Remix: Streaming UI with frames, stream a fallback first

cells.label: manual
cells.bodyHtml: No first-party preload Link headers or 103 Early Hints documented; the asset server returns module preloads that the document renders as <link rel="modulepreload"> tags. Set a Link header by hand on the returned Response. (assets, files-and-assets)
cells.exampleHtml:
There is no Early Hints API, so set a Link preload header yourself on the response the action returns.

// app/actions/books/controller.tsx
import { assets, stylesheetHref } from "../../assets.ts";

// inside the show action:
let coverHref = await assets.getHref("app/ui/public/cover.jpg");

return context.render(<BookPage book={book} coverHref={coverHref} />, {
  headers: {
    Link: [
      `<${stylesheetHref}>; rel=preload; as=style`,
      `<${coverHref}>; rel=preload; as=image; fetchpriority=high`,
    ].join(", "),
  },
});

Source: Remix: Rendering UI, rendering pages through request context

cells.label: first-party
cells.bodyHtml: Pages are server-rendered HTML; only components wrapped in clientEntry(import.meta.url, Component) hydrate. <Frame src="..." fallback={...}> streams a server-rendered region into the page and can load it lazily. (interactivity, streaming-ui-with-frames)
cells.exampleHtml:
Pages are server HTML. Only a component wrapped in clientEntry(import.meta.url, ...) is loaded and hydrated in the browser, with its props serialized into the page.

// app/actions/books/public/add-to-cart.tsx
import { clientEntry, on } from "remix/component";
import type { Handle } from "remix/component";

export const AddToCart = clientEntry(
  import.meta.url,
  function AddToCart(handle: Handle<{ bookId: string }>) {
    let added = false;
    return () => (
      <button
        type="button"
        mix={on("click", () => {
          added = true;
          handle.update();
        })}
      >
        {added ? "Added" : "Add to cart"}
      </button>
    );
  },
);

Source: Remix: Interactivity, hydration boundaries with clientEntry

cells.label: manual
cells.bodyHtml: Routes render on the server per request. remix/spa runs a whole app as a client-rendered app; no per-route prerender or SPA switch is documented. (spa, request-handling)
cells.exampleHtml:
Every route renders per request. To serve one page as static HTML, render it once at startup with renderToString() and return the stored string from that route.

// app/router.ts
import { renderToString } from "remix/component/server";
import { render } from "remix/middleware/render";
import { createHtmlResponse } from "remix/response/html";
import { createRouter } from "remix/router";
import { assets } from "./assets.ts";
import { AboutPage } from "./actions/about-page.tsx";

// rendered once, when the server starts
const aboutHtml = await renderToString(<AboutPage />);

export const router = createRouter({ middleware: [render({ assets })] });

router.get("/about", () =>
  createHtmlResponse(aboutHtml, { headers: { "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=3600" } }),
);
// all other routes: context.render(...) on each request

Source: Remix: Streaming UI with frames, render the response as a stream

cells.label: manual
cells.bodyHtml: State is a plain variable and the component re-renders only when the app calls handle.update(); there are no signals and no dependency tracking. (interactivity, component)
cells.exampleHtml:
State is a plain variable in setup scope. The component renders again only when you call handle.update().

// app/ui/public/counter.tsx
import { on } from "remix/component";
import type { Handle } from "remix/component";

export function Counter(handle: Handle<{ initialCount: number }>) {
  let count = handle.props.initialCount;

  return () => (
    <button
      type="button"
      mix={on("click", () => {
        count++;
        handle.update();
      })}
    >
      Count: {count}
    </button>
  );
}

Source: Remix: Interactivity, state, updates, and post-render tasks

cells.label: manual
cells.bodyHtml: There are no bundles to analyze: the asset server compiles modules on request and the browser loads them one by one. remix assets lists every reachable file and remix assets inspect <url-or-file> explains one mapping; neither reports sizes. (files-and-assets, assets)
cells.exampleHtml:
There is no bundle. The remix assets CLI lists every file the browser can reach and explains one URL. It reads the assets section of remix.json and does not report sizes.

// remix.json
{
  "$schema": "./node_modules/remix/schema/remix.json",
  "assets": {
    "basePath": "/assets",
    "allowFiles": ["app/routes.ts", "app/**/public/**"],
    "allowPackages": ["remix"],
    "files": { "extensions": [".svg", ".png", ".jpg", ".woff2"] }
  }
}
npx remix assets                                   # URL -> file for every reachable file
npx remix assets inspect /assets/app/ui/public/cart.ts

Source: Remix: Files and assets, debug asset URLs with remix assets

cells.label: manual
cells.bodyHtml: No first-party script-loading strategy documented; add <script> tags to the document by hand. (rendering-ui)
cells.exampleHtml:
There is no script loader. Put the <script> tag in the document shell's <head> with async or defer.

// app/actions/document.tsx
export function Document(handle: Handle<DocumentProps>) {
  return () => (
    <html lang="en">
      <head>
        <meta charSet="utf-8" />
        <title>{handle.props.title ?? "Books"}</title>
        {/* … import map, module preloads, entry script */}
        <script async src="https://plausible.io/js/script.js" data-domain="books.example.com"></script>
      </head>
      <body>{handle.props.children}</body>
    </html>
  );
}

Source: Remix: Rendering UI, document shells and head content

cells.label: manual
cells.bodyHtml: The router is a Fetch handler. Node runs it through remix/node-fetch-server, and the docs show Bun, Deno and Cloudflare Worker entries; the static-file and compression middleware are Node-only. No Vercel or Netlify setup is documented, and the Production chapter covers the Node server. (request-handling, production, node-fetch-server)
cells.exampleHtml:
The router is a Fetch handler. Node wraps it with createRequestListener; Bun, Deno and Workers call router.fetch directly.

// server.ts (Node)
import * as http from "node:http";
import { createRequestListener } from "remix/node-fetch-server";
import { router } from "./app/router.ts";

http.createServer(createRequestListener(router.fetch)).listen(44100);

// server.ts (Bun)
Bun.serve({ port: 44100, fetch: (request) => router.fetch(request) });

// server.ts (Deno)
Deno.serve({ port: 44100 }, router.fetch);

// worker.ts (Cloudflare)
export default { fetch: (request) => router.fetch(request) } satisfies ExportedHandler;

Source: Remix: Request handling, alternate runtimes

cells.label: manual
cells.bodyHtml: No service worker support documented in the Remix 3 guides or API reference. Hand-write the worker, serve it through the asset server or a static route, and register it from a client entry. (files-and-assets)
cells.exampleHtml:
Write sw.js by hand, serve it from the root public/ directory with staticFiles() so its scope is /, and register it from the browser entry.

// app/router.ts
export const router = createRouter({
  middleware: [staticFiles("./public", { index: false }), render({ assets })],
});

// app/actions/public/entry.ts
import { run } from "remix/component";

let app = run({ /* loadModule, … */ });
await app.ready();

if ("serviceWorker" in navigator) {
  navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js");
}

Source: Remix: Request handling, common middleware

methodology.disclaimerHtml: AI-generated note: This document was drafted with AI assistance and checked against vendor documentation. It is a check of capability only: nothing here was measured or benchmarked. Capability is described as of the versions in Versions checked for the nine main-table columns, and the Version line under each framework in Additional frameworks for the ten additional frameworks. Setup links point to vendor documentation and were link-checked on 2026-11-24. Claims flagged as uncertain are listed in Lower-confidence claims.
methodology.labelsHtml:
• ✅ 1st-party / built-in — the framework covers it with a default, a stable flag, or an official module/package from the framework team. Whether it is on by default or added as a module does not matter: @nuxt/image, @sveltejs/enhanced-img, and next/image all count the same.
  • 🧪 Experimental / third-party — the only path is a first-party API marked experimental or unstable, or a community package maintained outside the framework team.
  • 🔧 Manual — nothing covers it; the app (or this repo) wires it by hand, or goes without.

🧪 third-party applies when a community package or host service usable with that framework provides the feature itself (not just a building block the app still assembles by hand), whether or not the vendor docs mention it; each such entry names it. Partytown is credited only where the framework's own docs point to it.

The labels describe framework capability, not what a particular port chose. Opt-in is not a penalty. Several ports took a manual or third-party route even where a first-party primitive existed; the feature sections below call that out and link the vendor docs for each framework.

Rubric change: these labels follow a revised rubric (opt-in is no longer penalized; 🔶 and ❌ are removed), so scores are not comparable with earlier versions of this file.

Evidence: Each framework entry links the vendor docs for its label; 🔧 (and 🧪 third-party) entries link the docs page that covers the topic without a first-party primitive (worded "no first-party X documented", not "cannot"). Some labels follow the project owner's rubric decision rather than a literal reading of the linked docs; those cells are listed in Lower-confidence claims.
methodology.scoringHtml:
✅ = 2 points, 🧪 = 1, 🔧 = 0. Each table ends with a score row, which is the sum of its column. To recompute one by hand, read down a column and add:

Next, first table Label Points
Production CSS inlining 🧪 1
Font optimization ✅ 2
Image pipeline ✅ 2
Data/HTML caching ✅ 2
Route prefetching ✅ 2
Streaming SSR ✅ 2
Early Hints / preload headers ✅ 2
Total 13

That matches the 13 in the score row. The second table works the same way over eight rows (max 16), and the ranking adds the two totals.
methodology.rankingHtml:
How to read the ranking

Completeness % = (critical-path levers + other features) / 30, rounded to a whole percent. It measures the breadth of first-party and ecosystem performance features: items are unweighted, rows are not normalized against each other, and the islands row merges partial hydration, server islands, and lazy slices (best label). No measurements are used. Ties share a rank (2, 2, 4) and keep the earlier column order. Scores use the revised rubric and are not comparable with earlier versions.

How to recompute it

  1. Score each cell: ✅ = 2, 🧪 = 1, 🔧 = 0.
  2. Sum each table's column to get the score row (max 14 for the critical-path levers, max 16 for the other features).
  3. Add the two scores for the total (max 30), then divide by 30 for the completeness percentage. For example, Pracht: 14 + 12 = 26, and 26 / 30 rounds to 87%.

Treat this as a rough capability count only, not a performance prediction.
methodology.otherFeaturesSummaryHtml:
Summary: Nuxt has the widest set (13 of 16); Next, SvelteKit, and Pracht follow with 12. Nuxt has per-route rules, documented lazy hydration and experimental islands (🧪), modern-format images, first-party reactivity, an experimental analyzer, an official script module, Nitro presets, and a community PWA module. Pracht is the only framework where islands are a per-route hydration mode, and it also has server islands, ISG, an analyzer, a script component with loading strategies, and first-party adapters. TanStack Start has per-route SSR control, experimental deferred hydration (🧪), and (React only) experimental Server Components. SvelteKit has strong routing and deploy primitives and the only first-party service worker build in this table, but no islands and no built-in script or analysis tooling. SolidStart has the same gaps in script and analysis tooling, but gets modern-format <picture> output from the Solid team's @solidjs/image and experimental server components in Solid 2 (🧪); its deploy targets rely on Nitro and host-maintained plugins (🧪). Waku gets per-route rendering, adapters, lazy slices, and the React Compiler. Ember has autotracking and only a community analyzer beyond that.

The honest reading is that Next's strength is server rendering, not breadth. It has React Server Components, Cache Components/PPR, and cache tags, which these tables do not try to score. It scores 🔧 on art-direction ergonomics and 🧪 on deploy adapters.
methodology.additionalFrameworksHtml:
Labels for these ten frameworks come from vendor documentation and the package registry (npm; JSR for Fresh), at the versions listed under each framework, using the same legend and scoring as above. Ports of the first six now exist (astro-books, react-router-books, qwik-books, angular-books, marko-books, fresh-books; see the README for repos and deploys), each with a main baseline and an optimized branch (cache + self-hosted fonts) deployed to Vercel, Netlify, and Cloudflare. The labels below were not derived from those ports.

Analog, Vike, RedwoodSDK and Remix 3 have no Books port yet. They have no repo, no deploys, and no benchmark or FCP data; only the labels, links and versions below exist for them.

Why these frameworks: widely used alternatives with an SSR/SSG story. Analog is the Angular meta-framework, Vike is a Vite meta-framework with React, Vue and Solid renderers, RedwoodSDK is a React Server Components framework for Cloudflare Workers, and Remix 3 (npm remix 3.x) is a new framework with its own component runtime and no React, so it is scored separately from React Router. Not included: Gatsby, Eleventy, Remix v2 (superseded by React Router), HonoX (0.1.x; its README says it is in alpha and may break without a major release), and SvelteKit-adjacent projects.
lowerConfidenceClaims: TanStack Start (Solid)'s <Hydrate> guide has prose copied from the React variant, and its runtime behavior was not confirmed by building the Solid port.
TanStack Start (Solid) has no ISR guide; its caching label leans on the React ISR guide and the static-prerendering docs.

The 🧪 third-party labels for the TanStack ports' fonts, images, and analysis, and the 🔧 label for scripts, mean the docs make no first-party mention — not that these cannot be added by hand. The TanStack production checklist only tells readers to inspect fonts, images, and third-party scripts, not to use a primitive.

TanStack Start and SolidStart multi-host deployment (🧪): Nitro is a separate project and the Cloudflare and Netlify Vite plugins are host-maintained, although the TanStack hosting guide and the Solid deployment docs present them as the official setups. Scored ✅ on that basis, as before this revision, each of the three columns would gain 1 point.

The TanStack Start (Solid) doc links are the latest guides, which describe the v1 line (npm latest 1.169.7, Solid 1, vite-plugin-solid); the port runs @tanstack/solid-start 2.0.0-rc.8 on Solid 2 RC with @solidjs/vite-plugin, and tanstack.com publishes no separate v2 docs. The cited APIs (Hydrate, server.build.inlineCss, route ssr and headers, defaultPreload) were confirmed present in the 2.0.0-rc.8 packages, but the guides may not describe that line exactly.
Waku scripts (🔧): the linked migration page does not mention third-party scripts; the label rests on no primitive being documented there.

Ember's 🔧 cells (CSS, scripts) and 🧪 third-party cells (fonts, images via the community @responsive-image/ember, analysis) rest on the absence of a first-party primitive: the Ember Vite guide covers build setup only; the guides' only CSS and asset material is a generic HTML/CSS/JavaScript primer and the tutorial's CSS-and-assets section (app/styles/app.css, public/ for images and fonts); Embroider's Analyzing Bundles page defers to Vite tooling. The older cli.emberjs.com asset-compilation page is deprecated and covers the classic pipeline, so it is not cited.

Cells where the project owner's label differs from what the linked docs show (kept as given): SolidStart per-route render modes ✅ (an app-level Nitro prerender list plus Nitro routeRules; Nitro is not a Solid-team package and there is no per-route SSR/SPA switch); Next and Pracht art direction 🔧 (stable first-party getImageProps() helpers exist; scored 🔧 because neither ships a <picture>-emitting component); Waku data caching ✅ (waku-cache is a separate, still-evolving package, and the migration guide says to add caching explicitly); Ember data caching 🔧 (WarpDrive ships a first-party client request cache, docs). In the Data/HTML caching row, ✅ is given where vendor docs describe build-time prerender or static output plus response cache headers, even with no framework data cache (SvelteKit, TanStack Start, React Router, Qwik City, Angular). SolidStart is 🧪 because its cache (Nitro routeRules and defineCachedHandler) comes from Nitro, which the Solid team does not maintain; counted as first-party, as the Solid docs present Nitro, it would gain 1 point. Marko and Fresh stay 🔧 because they document only a hand-set Cache-Control header (Marko's static adapter exports the whole app and does not cache a server-rendered one).

Nuxt lazy hydration is on by default and documented without a warning on the components page, but its config key is experimental.lazyHydration on the Experimental Features page; the islands cell is 🧪 on that basis, as are experimental server components and <NuxtIsland>.

Nuxt bundle analysis 🧪: the nuxt analyze command is documented as experimental; the build.analyze config option carries no experimental label but, with the Vite builder, relies on the community rollup-plugin-visualizer being installed. If that flag were counted as a stable first-party path the cell would be ✅ and Nuxt's total 25 (83%, tied with Next and SvelteKit at rank 3).

@sveltejs/enhanced-img is 1.0.1 on npm and the svelte.dev images page carries no experimental label, but the package README (npm and GitHub main) still says "This package is experimental. It uses pre-1.0 versioning"; the SvelteKit image-pipeline and <picture> cells (✅) treat that README text as stale. Read literally, both cells would be 🧪 and SvelteKit's total would be 23 (77%).
SolidStart image pipeline and <picture> (✅): @solidjs/image is a Solid-team package (GitHub solidjs/solid-image, npm) but is absent from docs.solidjs.com; the labels rest on the package README.

Astro, React Router, Qwik City, Angular, Marko and Fresh have main and optimized ports but are not in the Lighthouse runs yet; Analog, Vike, RedwoodSDK and Remix 3 have no port; every label is from vendor docs under the same rubric, not from the ports. Qwik and Astro rows were judged against the rubric as noted in their bullets.

Marko multi-host deployment (✅): the Cloudflare adapter is announced as official on markojs.com (October 2026 newsletter) but is not yet on the adapters page; the Vercel adapter is a first-party package documented only on npm and in the marko-js/run repo, not on markojs.com.
Marko data/HTML caching (🔧): if the app-wide @marko/run-adapter-static export were accepted as caching, the cell would be ✅ and Marko's first-table score would be 6 (total 13, 43%).

Qwik v2 (2.0.0-rc.5) differences are unverified; the Qwik labels use v1 docs. Qwik City 1.20.4 ships no Vercel Node/serverless adapter (vercel-edge only); a cloudflare-workers adapter is documented alongside cloudflare-pages and reuses the same adapter code.
Fresh build-time prerender exists only as an open PR and is not credited.

Fresh multi-host deployment (🔧) is a judgment from the documented hosts, as for Angular: Deno Deploy, deno compile, Docker and Cloudflare Workers (through Cloudflare's own @cloudflare/vite-plugin) are documented, but Node, Vercel and Netlify are not. Counting the Cloudflare page as third-party coverage would make this cell 🧪 and Fresh's second-table score 6.

Angular multi-host portability (🔧) is a judgment: Node is first-party and Netlify and Cloudflare SSR are host-maintained, but no Vercel SSR path is documented, so the cell is scored like Fresh (partial host coverage). If three of four hosts were accepted as 🧪, Angular's total would be 19 (63%). Angular font optimization (🧪): optimization.fonts.inline is first-party but only inlines the Google/Adobe font CSS; if that counted as font optimization the cell would be ✅ and Angular's total 19 (63%).

Angular bundle analysis (🧪): the --stats-json flag, the build size summary and size budgets are first-party and stable; only the module-level viewer (esbuild's analyze page) is external. Pracht is scored ✅ for a first-party size report plus budgets, so if that standard is applied Angular's cell becomes ✅ and its total 19 (63%).

React Router multi-host (🧪) is a judgment: Node, Cloudflare, and AWS adapters are maintained by the React Router team, while Vercel and Netlify are host-maintained; read literally, the rubric could give ✅.
Marko Run is 0.x (0.11.19 on npm; 0.11.17 in the port), pre-1.0.

Ember per-route render modes (🔧): community vite-ember-ssr can prerender a listed set of routes (emberSsg({ routes })), the same mechanism that earns React Router and SolidStart their ✅ when first-party. Credited as a community package it would be 🧪, giving Ember 6 (20%), still last.

React Router naming: "v7" in older material is the same framework mode that docs now call v8 (npm latest 8.5.2); the how-to pages give no minimum versions, but the changelog dates the prerender config to v7.0.0, unstable RSC Data Mode APIs to v7.7.0, and unstable RSC Framework Mode to v7.9.2.
Angular incremental-hydration and route-level render-mode stability (stable since v20) comes from the Angular roadmap, not from the guides.

Not found in the docs, and not affecting any label: Angular's default router preloading strategy (not stated on the fetched page), the behaviour of Astro's security.csp (unscored extra), and whether a Vite ?inline CSS import works in Fresh.

Streaming SSR for Waku (✅): waku.gg has no streaming section. The label rests on the redirects and not-found guide, which describes behavior "inside a Suspense boundary after the shell has already been sent", and on React Server Components streaming by design.

Streaming SSR for Qwik City (✅) is in-order streaming with deferred loaders. Out-of-order streaming exists only in the Qwik v2 release candidate's labs docs and is not credited. Astro is also in-order; both are ✅ because the row asks only that the shell is flushed before slow data.
Streaming SSR for Angular, Fresh, and Ember (🔧) rests on the SSR docs describing no streamed page render. Angular's guide and Fresh's docs never say that streaming is unsupported.

Early Hints / preload headers for Next (✅): the reactMaxHeadersLength page says React emits preload headers "during prerendering" and that Next adds them to the response. It does not say whether fully dynamic responses get them, and Next documents no 103 of its own. Read as experimental-grade coverage the cell would be 🧪 and Next's total 24 (80%).

Early Hints / preload headers for SvelteKit and Pracht (✅): both add preload Link headers for built assets; only Pracht's Node adapter and Nuxt's experimental flag write a 103 from the framework. If the row required the framework to send the 103 on every host, SvelteKit would be 🔧 and Pracht would keep ✅ on Node only.

Early Hints / preload headers 🔧 cells (SolidStart, Waku, Ember, Astro, React Router, Qwik City, Angular, Marko, Fresh, Analog, RedwoodSDK, Remix 3) rest on the absence of a documented primitive. Cloudflare's Early Hints feature converts a cached Link header into a 103 on any framework; it is a host building block that still needs the app to set the header, so it is not credited as 🧪 third-party.

Service worker 🧪 third-party cells follow one rule: a framework-specific community package earns the credit (Serwist for Next, @vite-pwa/nuxt, @vite-pwa/astro), and the generic vite-plugin-pwa does not, because an SSR app still wires the navigation fallback by hand. Under a looser rule every Vite-based column (SolidStart, TanStack Start, Pracht, Waku, React Router, Marko, Fresh, Analog, Vike, RedwoodSDK) would be 🧪 and gain 1 point. Remix 3 has no Vite build.

Service worker for Qwik City (🧪 experimental): @qwikdev/pwa is published by the QwikDev org but is 0.0.4, was last published on 2024-02-26, and is not in the qwik.dev docs. If it is not accepted the cell is 🔧 and Qwik City's total 22 (73%).

Service worker for Ember (🔧): ember-service-worker 9.0.1 (2020) targets the classic Ember CLI pipeline. Counted as a community package the cell would be 🧪 and Ember's total 6 (20%). Service worker for React Router (🔧): @vite-pwa/remix targets Remix and was not confirmed against React Router v8.

Links for the three rows added on 2026-11-25 (streaming SSR, Early Hints / preload headers, service worker / offline support) were checked on that date. The ports were not changed for these rows, so none of the new snippets comes from a port. The Analog, Vike, RedwoodSDK and Remix 3 cells for these rows were read from the vendor docs on 2026-11-26.
Next worker strategy and Bun adapter status are taken from the linked docs as of this edit; Cloudflare/Netlify verified adapters are described there as in progress.

The linked Pracht docs are unversioned, so they describe the current release (1.0.1, which the port runs). Several ports pin pre-release builds: Nuxt (4.6.0 nightly on the optimized branches), Waku (1.0.0-rc.5, the newest release), TanStack Start Solid (2.0.0-rc.8), and the SolidStart pieces (Solid 2 RC, Nitro 3 beta). @tanstack/react-start itself is on stable 1.169.x, but both TanStack ports use a Nitro 3 beta. Vendor docs can change week to week.

SolidStart is not @solidjs/start here: Solid 2 (port pinned to 2.0.0-rc.6; 2.0.3 is npm latest) in @solidjs/vite-plugin start mode plus Nitro 3 beta. SolidStart v2 itself is stable on Solid 1 and its docs are at v1.solidjs.com. The doc links in this file are references, not a description of this port's build. Links to v1.solidjs.com describe released SolidStart v2 / Solid Router v1; links to docs.solidjs.com describe Solid 2 start mode.

No code example was found in the repo or the linked docs for: CSS inlining for Waku and Ember; images for Waku and Ember; prefetching for Ember; islands for SolidStart and Ember; Next islands (prose only; the flag snippet is in section 4); Next and Ember per-route render modes; <picture> for SolidStart, TanStack Start (React and Solid), Pracht, Waku, and Ember; TanStack Start (React) and Pracht reactivity; bundle analysis for SvelteKit, SolidStart, TanStack Start, Waku, and Ember; third-party scripts for SvelteKit, SolidStart, Waku, and Ember; multi-host deployment for Ember; streaming SSR for Waku and Ember; Early Hints / preload headers for Waku and Ember; service workers for SolidStart, TanStack Start (React and Solid), Pracht, Waku, and Ember. The TanStack Start (Solid) streaming and Early Hints entries, and its caching, prefetching, scripts, and deployment entries reuse the React snippet instead of repeating it, and its reactivity entry reuses the SolidStart one.
Analog, Vike, RedwoodSDK and Remix 3 have no Books port, so none of their labels was tried in a build. Every label is read from the vendor docs at the version on the framework's Version line.

Analog image pipeline, route prefetching, islands and reactivity (✅) rest on Angular-team packages (NgOptimizedImage, router preloading, incremental hydration, signals), following the rule that credits React Compiler to the React meta-frameworks. The Analog docs mention incremental hydration and signals but not NgOptimizedImage or withPreloading. If only Analog-team packages counted, the image and prefetching cells would be 🧪 and Analog's total 15 (50%).

Analog CSS inlining (🔧): the Analog docs list no critical-CSS option, and Angular CLI's inlineCritical belongs to the angular.json build that Analog replaces with Vite. Whether an Analog build can run that step was not confirmed.

Vike data/HTML caching (✅) rests on stable build-time pre-rendering; +headersResponse is marked beta and ISR is Vercel-only through vite-plugin-vercel. Vike multi-host (🧪) follows the TanStack Start and React Router cells: the Cloudflare, Netlify and Vercel plugins are not vike packages, although the Vike docs present them as the standard setup. Scored ✅, Vike's total would be 17 (57%).
Vike is 0.4.x and its React, Vue and Solid extensions are 0.x; the docs do not call the core experimental, so no cell is marked 🧪 for that.

RedwoodSDK per-route render modes (✅) covers client-only and static-HTML route groups; there is no build-time prerender. RedwoodSDK image pipeline (🧪) names Cloudflare Images, which the RedwoodSDK docs do not mention. RedwoodSDK data/HTML caching (🔧) is scored like Fresh: only hand-set headers are documented.

Remix 3 CSS inlining (✅) covers styles written with the css(...) mixin; a global stylesheet is still a linked file. If only whole-stylesheet inlining counted, the cell would be 🔧 and Remix 3's total 8 (27%).

Remix 3 image pipeline (🧪): the transform pipeline, URL syntax and file cache are first-party, but the resize code is written by the app with Sharp. Counting the pipeline alone would make the cell ✅ and the total 11 (37%).

Remix 3 reactivity, bundle analysis, render modes and multi-host (🔧) rest on the docs describing a different model (explicit handle.update(), unbundled modules, per-request rendering) or documenting no primitive. The Remix docs name Node, Bun, Deno and Cloudflare Workers; if that counted as partial host coverage the multi-host cell would be 🧪.
Analog streaming SSR (🧪 experimental): the Analog page calls it experimental and opt-in. Counted as stable it would be ✅ and Analog's total 18 (60%).

Vike Early Hints (✅): Vike computes the asset list (pageContext.httpResponse.earlyHints), but the app's server writes the 103; Vike documents no preload Link response header. TanStack Start's onEarlyHints hook works the same way and is 🧪 only because it is marked experimental. If the row required the framework to send the 103 or the header itself, the cell would be 🔧 and Vike's total 14 (47%).

Analog service worker (🔧): @angular/service-worker is an Angular-team package, but its asset manifest comes from the Angular CLI build, which Analog replaces with Vite, and the Analog docs do not cover it. Credited like Analog's other Angular-team cells, it would be ✅ and Analog's total 19 (63%).
Several snippets are shortened (marked "omitted" or "abridged" in their captions) and some doc snippets are adapted from short quotes.
